SHANNON, Ireland, Sept 13 (Reuters) – U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday said he would consider a request from relatives of those killed in the September 11 attacks to release more records about the event.

“I’m going to look at it when I get back,” he told reporters in Ireland before boarding a plane to fly back to the United States.

Centre-left bloc leads in Swedish vote, polls show

Reuters

14 September, 2026 01:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Anna Ringstrom and Simon Johnson STOCKHOLM, Sept 13 (Reuters) – Sweden’s centre-left parties, which back Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson for prime minister, held an early lead with 51.3% of the vote in a parliamentary election on Sunday, an exit poll by broadcaster SVT showed.

Early results from the Swedish Election Authority are expected within hours after polls closed at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT). A separate election-day poll conducted by broadcaster TV4 also showed the centre-left in the lead.

If the centre-left’s lead is confirmed by official results, it would halt Sweden’s recent rightward drift away from its liberal traditions in an election that many analysts viewed as a referendum on the Sweden Democrats, a grouping with roots in the neo-Nazi fringe.

Show Full Article

Swedish exit polls, while often indicative of the final outcome, have not always proved accurate. In 2022, an exit poll projected Andersson’s bloc would prevail, but the election was ultimately won by a right-wing coalition headed by Ulf Kristersson, who is now Sweden’s prime minister.

As exit poll readings were broadcast, cheering broke out at the election gatherings of the centre-left parties while the outcome was met with silence among the far-right Sweden Democrats, with the exit polls indicating a setback after they boosted their vote share over several consecutive elections.

“If this holds up, Magdalena Andersson will become our country’s prime minister,” the Social Democrats’ party secretary Tobias Baudin told SVT after the exit poll results were announced.

The SVT exit poll gave the centre-left bloc 183 seats, above the 175 needed for a majority, while the right-wing parties were set to win 166 seats.

“There is a wish for a kind of change,” Marie Demker, professor of political science at Gothenburg University, said.

“How that change is going to work out with these different red lines that these parties have drawn is tomorrow’s worry.”

Many Swedes have expressed wariness over Kristersson’s push towards strict migration limits and saw his pre-election promise to bring the Sweden Democrats into government as a step too far.

“This is not what we hoped for, but it’s not the final results so we’ll have to see,” the Sweden Democrats deputy party leader Henrik Vinge told TV4.

“You typically see some decline when you’re part of the ruling coalition,” he said.

Kristersson, who has trailed in opinion polls throughout his four years in office, had been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning, with Andersson and her Social Democrats losing ground.

Critics say Kristersson’s government is undermining civil liberties while forcing immigrants to conform more closely to Swedish cultural norms or leave the country, urged on by both inducements and penalties.

Electoral success for the Sweden Democrats would be welcomed by Europe’s ascendant far-right parties, which were bolstered by the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany’s win in a German state election last week.

The far right hopes for gains in upcoming elections across Europe, with the National Rally’s bid for the French presidency next year potentially its biggest prize.

(Reporting by Niklas Pollard, Simon Johnson, Johan Ahlander and Tom Little; additional reporting by Ilze Filks, Ardee Napolitano, Janis Laizans for Reuters TV, Greta Rosen Fondahn, Marie Mannes, Terje Solsvik and Anna Ringstrom; Writing by Niklas Pollard and Justyna Pawlak; Editing by Peter Graff, Philippa Fletcher and Edmund Klamann)

Ukraine’s Zelenskiy imposes sanctions on former press secretary

Reuters

14 September, 2026 12:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

KYIV, Sept 13 (Reuters) – Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskiy imposed sanctions on a former press secretary on Sunday, accusing her and nine others of spreading Russian propaganda and of supporting Russia’s aggressive policy toward Ukraine.

Yuliia Mendel — who worked with Zelenskiy from 2019 to 2021, before Russia’s invasion — responded with a message on Facebook saying it was unconstitutional to impose sanctions on Ukrainian citizens. She did not comment on the specific accusations.

Mendel has given interviews criticising Zelenskiy’s record since last year, when a number of members of the president’s inner circle became embroiled in corruption scandals. The suspects have denied the charges that have not been tested in court.

Show Full Article

The sanctions — announced by Zelenskiy in a decree — would last for 10 years and included asset freezes and restrictions on trade, the document read.

They were an unusual measure to use against a former member of staff, though they have been used against political figures.

In 2025, Ukraine imposed sanctions on former president and opposition politician Petro Poroshenko, including an asset freeze and a ban on withdrawing capital from the country, for what the domestic spy agency said were “national security” reasons.

Sunday’s order “imposes restrictions on 10 Russian and Ukrainian individuals who spread disinformation and Russian propaganda and support Russia’s aggressive policy toward Ukraine. Yuliia Mendel is among those sanctioned,” the presidency said in a statement.

Mendel, Zelenskiy’s first press secretary after he became president, wrote on Facebook that she had been expecting the move.

“Sanctions against Ukrainian citizens are unconstitutional, as are many of Zelenskiy’s other decisions,” she added. “Volodymyr Zelenskiy is imposing them on anyone who advocates for peace in Ukraine.”

(Reporting by Pavel Polityuk; Editing by Andrew Heavens)
